procedural_history.originating_court: Court of Presidency Magistrate at Calcutta
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated the 12th March 1952 of the Court of Presidency Magistrate at Calcutta in Case No. C/2867 of 1950.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The order of the Presidency Magistrate was challenged in the Calcutta High Court by way of Criminal Revision No. 312 of 1952. The High Court issued a Judgment and Order dated 4th July 1952.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The case reached the Supreme Court via a Special Leave Petition, which was converted into Criminal Appeals Nos. 67 and 68 of 1954. The appellant was challenging the High Court's Judgment and Order.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code is unconstitutional and violative of Article 14 for vesting an arbitrary and discriminatory power in the government to grant or withhold sanction for the prosecution of a public servant.

law.name: Section 197, Criminal Procedure Code
law.description: Requires prior sanction from the government to prosecute a public servant for an offence alleged to have been committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty.

law.name: Article 14, Constitution of India
law.description: Guarantees the right to equality and prohibits the state from denying any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws.

application.description: The Court first determined that the distinction made by Section 197 between public servants and other citizens is based on a 'rational classification'.

It reasoned that this classification is justified because public servants require protection from harassment that could arise from actions taken in the discharge of their official duties, a safeguard that ordinary citizens do not need.

The Court distinguished between discretionary power and discriminatory power, stating that a discretionary power is not necessarily a discriminatory one. It held that abuse of power should not be easily assumed, especially when the discretion is vested in the government rather than a minor official.

The Court also found no discrimination against the complainants. It argued that the rule requiring sanction applies equally to all persons wishing to prosecute a public servant. It suggested that only a public servant against whom sanction is granted (while it is withheld for another) could possibly complain of discrimination, but that was not the position of the petitioners in this case.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge, holding that Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code is not unconstitutional or violative of Article 14. The Court found that the requirement for sanction is based on a rational classification that protects public servants from harassment and that the discretionary power given to the government is not inherently discriminatory.

issue.issue_text: Whether the necessity for sanction under Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code must be determined only at the initial stage of the proceedings.

law.text: The need for sanction under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not necessarily to be considered as soon as the complaint is lodged.
The question of whether sanction is necessary may arise and have to be determined at any stage of the proceedings, from stage to stage.

application.text: The Court reasoned that a complaint, at its initial filing, may not disclose that the alleged offense was committed by a public servant while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of their official duty.
Facts that establish the necessity for sanction might only emerge later, such as during a police or judicial inquiry, or even in the course of the prosecution's evidence at trial.

The Court acknowledged that some prior judgments appeared to support the view that the issue must be decided at the earliest stage. However, it clarified that a careful reading of those judgments shows they did not intend to establish such a rigid rule, as they also contemplated that proceedings could be dropped later if the connection to official duty was established.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the need for sanction must be determined only at the initial stage. It held that the court can and must consider the question at any stage of the proceedings, as the facts establishing the necessity for sanction may only reveal themselves as the case progresses.

issue.issue_text: Whether officials conducting a lawful search have the right to use reasonable force to remove obstruction or resistance, or if their only remedy is to file a complaint with the police or a magistrate.

facts: Officials were authorized by a warrant to conduct a search.
During the search, they were met with obstruction and resistance by individuals at the premises.
The appellants argued that the officials had no right to use force to remove the obstruction and that their only legal option was to file a complaint with the police or a magistrate.
law: The Court cited the legal principle, supported by Broom's Legal Maxims, that "when the law commands a thing to be done, it authorises the performance of whatever may be necessary for executing its command."

This means that when a power is conferred or a duty is imposed by law, it implicitly includes the power to do all acts that are reasonably necessary to execute that power or duty, unless expressly restricted.
application: The Court applied this principle to the act of conducting a lawful search.
It reasoned that if officials encounter obstruction or resistance, they must have the right to use reasonable means to remove it in order to perform their duty.

The Court stated that denying officials this right would "frustrate the due discharge to the official duty and defeat the very object of the search," as it would give people time to hide or destroy evidence while the officials sought help.
Furthermore, it would encourage people to resist lawful acts.
The Court clarified that while the use of *more than reasonable* force could be a separate matter for inquiry, it does not make the act of removing the obstruction itself unlawful.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that officials' only remedy against obstruction is to file a complaint. It held that when officials are conducting a lawful search and encounter obstruction or resistance, they have the right to use reasonable force to remove that obstruction and carry out their duty.

issue.issue_text: Whether a bona fide mistake in the premises number on a search warrant renders the search illegal.

facts: A search warrant authorized a search of '17, Kalakar Street'.
The officials actually entered and searched 'P-17, Kalakar Street'.
The account books and other items sought by the warrant were found at P-17, the premises that were actually raided.
application: The court considered it probable that the warrant specified '17' instead of 'P. 17' due to a 'bona fide mistake or error'.
Alternatively, the court considered that the searching party may have made an 'honest mistake' in entering the wrong premises.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, finding the objection to be of 'no substance.' The court reasoned that the error was likely a bona fide or honest mistake, and this was supported by the fact that the relevant account books were actually found in the premises that were raided (P-17).

issue.issue_text: Whether a power conferred or a duty imposed on an official implies the power of employing all necessary means for its execution.

law.fact: The Court cited the legal principle that when a power is conferred or a duty is imposed by law, and there are no express limitations, it implicitly includes the power to do all acts or use all means that are reasonably necessary for its execution.
law.source: Where a power is conferred or a duty imposed by statute or otherwise, and there is nothing said expressly inhibiting the exercise of the power or the performance of the duty by any limitations or restrictions, it is reasonable to hold that it carries with it the power of doing all such acts or employing such means as are reasonably necessary for such execution .

law.fact: This principle is supported by a well-established rule stated in Broom's Legal Maxims.
law.source: The true position is neatly stated thus in Broom's Legal Maxims, 10th Ed., at page 312 : "It is a rule that when the law commands a thing to be done, it authorises the performance of whatever may be necessary for executing its command".

law.fact: The Court also noted that this principle aligns with common sense.
law.source: This accords with ~om­monsense and does not seem contrary to any principle of law.

application.fact: Applying this principle, the Court reasoned that if an official encounters obstruction or resistance while performing their duty, they have the right to use reasonable means to overcome that resistance.
application.source: If in the exercise of the power or the performance of the official duty, improper or unlawful obstruction or resistance is encountered, .. there must be the right to use reasonable means to remove the obstruction or overcome the resistance.

application.fact: The Court distinguished and found unhelpful two English cases that took a narrower view, such as one that held a power to apprehend a person did not include the power to move them gently aside.
application.source: The two English cases relied on are scarcely of any help. In Jones v. Owen('), a rather startling view was taken that a power to apprehend a person for a statu-tory offence did not include a power to move that person gently aside.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, holding that a power or duty conferred on an official implies the authority to use all reasonably necessary means for its execution. This conclusion is based on the legal maxim that a command by law authorizes whatever is necessary for its performance, a principle the Court found to be consistent with common sense.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the necessity for sanction under Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code must be determined only at the initial stage of the proceedings.
appellant_arguments: The court has a duty to allow the prosecution to proceed and should not dismiss it at the initial stage ('in limine') for lack of sanction.
respondent_arguments: The issue of sanction can and should be decided at the outset of the proceedings if the facts indicate the act was related to official duty.

arguments.issue_text: Whether officials conducting a lawful search have the right to use reasonable force to remove obstruction or resistance, or if their only remedy is to file a complaint with the police or a magistrate.
appellant_arguments: When officials face obstruction or resistance during a lawful search, they have no right to use force to remove it.
The only remedy available to the officials in such a situation is to file a complaint with the police or a magistrate.
respondent_arguments: Denying officials the right to use reasonable force would frustrate the discharge of their official duty and defeat the purpose of the search, as evidence could be destroyed in the interim.
Allowing only a complaint as a remedy would encourage obstruction of lawful acts.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a bona fide mistake in the premises number on a search warrant renders the search illegal.
appellant_arguments: The entry into the wrong premises (P-17 Kalakar Street instead of the authorized 17 Kalakar Street) rendered the search illegal from its very commencement.
respondent_arguments: The provided text does not explicitly state the respondent's argument, but implies they argued that a bona fide mistake in the address does not automatically render the search illegal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a power conferred or a duty imposed on an official implies the power of employing all necessary means for its execution.
appellant_arguments: The power to search does not imply the power to use force to overcome obstruction; the only recourse is a formal complaint.
respondent_arguments: The power to conduct a search must include the implied power to use necessary and reasonable means, such as force against obstruction, to effectively execute that duty.

cases.case_name: Hori Ram Singh v. The Crown
cases.principle: The test for whether an act requires sanction is whether the public servant can reasonably claim that what they did was done in virtue of their office.

cases.case_name: Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli v. The State of Bombay
cases.principle: Section 197 should not be construed too narrowly, as the focus is on the 'act' and not the 'duty', because an official act can be performed in the discharge of official duty as well as in dereliction of it.

cases.case_name: Amrik Singh v. The State of PEPSU
cases.principle: Sanction is necessary if the acts complained of are so integrally connected with the duties of the office as to be inseparable from them; no sanction is needed if the official status merely provided the opportunity for the acts.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where a power is conferred or a duty is imposed by statute, and there are no express limitations or restrictions inhibiting its exercise, it implicitly carries with it the power to do all acts or employ all means that are reasonably necessary for its execution.
obiter: The necessity for sanction against a public servant may not be apparent from the initial complaint but can arise at any stage of the proceedings as facts come to light, and the determination of whether it is required may have to be made from stage to stage.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that for a public servant to claim protection under Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, there must be a reasonable connection between the act complained of and the discharge of their official duty. This protection extends to acts involving the use of reasonable force to overcome obstruction during a lawful search, as the power to perform a duty implies the power to use all necessary means for its execution. The necessity for such sanction can be determined at any stage of the proceedings, and the provision itself is not unconstitutional, as the discretionary power vested in the government is not inherently discriminatory.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if an act falls under Section 197, the court must find a 'reasonable connection between the act and the discharge of official duty; the act must bear such relation to the duty that the accused could lay a reasonable, but not a pretended or fanciful claim, that he did it in the course of the performance of his duty.'

The court applied the principle of implied powers, stating: 'it is a rule that when the law commands a thing to be done, it authorises the performance of whatever may be necessary for executing its command.'
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the need for sanction should not be decided at the initial stage was rejected because the court found that the question 'may arise at any stage of the proceedings' and 'may have to be determined from stage to stage.'

The 'extreme proposition' that officials facing obstruction can only file a complaint and not use force was rejected, as such a view would 'frustrate the due discharge to the official duty and defeat the very object of the search.'
The claim that a bona fide mistake in the premises number on a search warrant rendered the search illegal was dismissed as an 'objection of no substance.'

The challenge to the constitutionality of Section 197 was dismissed because the court found 'no question of any discrimination' against complainants, as the sanction requirement applies universally to such cases, and 'a discretionary power is not necessarily a discriminatory power.'
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed that the necessity for sanction can be determined at any point, as 'facts subsequently coming to light on a police or judicial inquiry, or even in the course of the prosecution evidence at the trial, may establish the necessity for sanction.'

The court held that the power to conduct a search implies the right to execute it effectively, stating that when a duty is imposed, 'it carries with it the power of doing all such acts or employing such means as are reasonably necessary for such execution.'

The court found that even if the officials' belief that they could use force was mistaken, they could 'reasonably claim that what they did was in virtue of their official duty,' thus connecting the act to their official capacity.

The court upheld Section 197 by reasoning that the discretionary power to grant sanction is vested in the government, not a minor official, and 'abuse of power is not to be easily assumed' in such circumstances.
policy_considerations: Allowing officials to only file a complaint when obstructed would 'frustrate the due discharge to the official duty and defeat the very object of the search, as the books, etc. might be secreted or destroyed in the interval; and it would encourage obstruction or resistance even to lawful acts.'

The court expressed a policy of deference to high-level executive discretion, stating that 'abuse of power is not to be easily assumed where the discretion is vested in the government and not in a minor official.'
